title: #52 Introduce Checks for Listening Using Non-Subject Content
author: Barton, Craig
summary: Barton addresses the common failure mode where a "check for listening" collapses into a check for subject understanding, so students who have already switched off (often from low confidence) cannot demonstrate they were paying attention. He illustrates this with "Tom," a maths student who tunes out because he expects to fail, and who therefore cannot answer even a simple repeat-back question about the teacher's explanation. Barton then describes a coaching observation of a teacher who instead ran a preliminary listening check using entirely unrelated trivia -- the colours of the Swedish flag, Newcastle United's FA Cup wins -- before starting the actual maths explanation. Because the trivia carries no subject-matter anxiety, every student can succeed, which lets the teacher explicitly frame listening as separate from understanding. The tip's underlying claim is that by decoupling the check from content difficulty, teachers remove the confidence barrier that causes low-attainers to disengage, and can then hold the whole class accountable for listening before any content-specific stakes are in play.
points: Checks for listening that use actual subject content conflate listening with understanding, so students who have already given up on the content fail even though they may have been listening.
Barton's "Tom" example shows how a lack of subject confidence causes a student to switch off before an explanation even starts, making any content-based listening check useless for him.

The fix: open with a listening check built entirely from non-subject trivia (flag colours, football history) so every student can succeed regardless of ability, then explicitly tell students the difference between listening and understanding.
Removing the content barrier lets a teacher establish whole-class attention and accountability before the stakes of the actual lesson content are introduced.
quotes: I have previously written about the need to regularly check students are listening to our explanations and instructions.
Tom gets confused, concludes this is yet another area of maths he is doomed to fail at, and promptly switches off.
Tom’s teacher checks Tom is listening by asking him to repeat the first step he has just explained.
Because Tom has switched off, he is unable to answer this question. And, of course, if Tom is not listening, he will never understand.
Now, you all got those questions correct because you were listening. I am now going to explain something else, and check you are listening in just the same way.

By introducing students to checks for listening for non-subject content, the teacher was able to remove any barriers to listening that a lack of confidence with subject content might bring, and ensure he had everyone’s attention.
